justifications.functional_suitability: All functional requirements are comprehensively met: Fraud Scoring Engine scores transactions (R-01), Case Management API & UI supports analyst workflows (R-02), and Rule/Model Authoring Service enables zero-downtime updates via SQS distribution (R-03).
justifications.performance_efficiency: The sub-50ms P99 target at 3,000 rps is supported by Netty/WebFlux, in-memory embedded ONNX runtime, local Caffeine/Redis caching in Feature Enriched Component, DynamoDB lookups, and asynchronous offloading of audit logs and case reviews.
justifications.compatibility: The architecture cleanly interfaces with external Payment Gateways using industry-standard gRPC and REST over TLS 1.3/mTLS, and integrates smoothly with standard AWS platform APIs and identity systems.
justifications.usability: Fraud Analysts and Operations Managers are provided a dedicated React SPA with WebSockets. Rule authors and data scientists have specialized authoring and simulation endpoints, while compliance auditors have dedicated audit access paths.
justifications.reliability: High availability and R-07 fail-open requirements are explicitly addressed by the Resilience4j Circuit Breaker & Fallback Component, AWS ALB health-check target groups, and asynchronous decoupling with Amazon SQS.
justifications.security: Strong security with mTLS, WAF, KMS CMKs, and 7-year S3 Object Lock. However, attributing card tokenization directly to the native AWS ALB is technically unrealistic without an explicit tokenization proxy or Lambda@Edge component.
justifications.maintainability: Modular domain segregation into dedicated microservices (scoring, authoring, case management) and serverless AWS components (Fargate, DynamoDB, SQS) minimizes operational maintenance overhead, fitting the three-engineer team constraint well.
justifications.portability: While perfectly aligned with the AWS eu-west-1 target, the solution exhibits strong vendor lock-in to proprietary AWS services (DynamoDB Streams, S3 Object Lock, SQS, KMS, Fargate), making migration to another environment difficult.

PERF-01.justification: Spring WebFlux with embedded ONNX Runtime and Caffeine feature caching supports sub-50ms execution. However, synchronous DynamoDB writes for entity state and audit records at 3,000 rps introduce latency jitter that could threaten P99 latency.
sensitivity_points: Synchronous DynamoDB round-trips in the critical path
Local memory and cache hit ratios for feature enrichment
tradeoffs: Synchronous state persistence improves consistency but risks P99 latency degradation

PERF-02.justification: Case management is completely decoupled from the real-time scoring path. Review cases are routed asynchronously via Amazon SQS to a dedicated Case Management service, ensuring heavy analyst querying has zero performance impact on authorization scoring.
sensitivity_points: SQS queue ingestion throughput under peak review volume
tradeoffs: Asynchronous case routing guarantees isolation but introduces eventual consistency for review availability

AVAIL-01.justification: Resilience4j provides container-level fallback logic for internal errors. However, if the entire container crashes or ECS fails, AWS ALB lacks an automated edge fail-open bypass mechanism to approve or route payments within one minute.
sensitivity_points: ALB fail-open routing configuration when target health checks fail
tradeoffs: Failing open preserves payment processing availability but temporarily accepts unverified fraud risks

AVAIL-02.justification: The Audit Logger uses an internal blocking queue and synchronous writes to DynamoDB. If the storage layer degrades, backpressure in the blocking queue can stall scoring threads or drop audit events without a dedicated decoupled buffer.
sensitivity_points: Blocking queue capacity and eviction policies under downstream audit storage latency
tradeoffs: Non-blocking audit buffering prevents scoring thread starvation but risks memory exhaustion during outages

MOD-01.justification: The Rule/Model Authoring Service validates and signs models, deploying via SQS and dynamic updates without container restart. ECS rolling deployments and model version tagging in decision outputs are well-supported, enabling fast rollback.
sensitivity_points: Dynamic runtime model swapping without worker thread interruption
tradeoffs: Embedded runtime model switching avoids restarts but increases heap and runtime complexity

MOD-02.justification: New rules are validated via Drools, simulated using serverless workers, and published to DynamoDB and SQS without downtime. The Explainability Formatter records rule outcomes in decision metadata, fully satisfying the 1-hour activation requirement.
sensitivity_points: Validation and dry-run execution speed in simulation workers
tradeoffs: Pre-deployment dry-run simulations slow down rapid publishing but prevent erroneous rule propagation

SEC-01.justification: ALB tokenization and role segregation prevent analysts from accessing raw PANs. However, while audit logging is present, the architecture lacks SIEM, behavioral analytics, or intrusion alerting to detect and alert anomalous access within 15 minutes.
sensitivity_points: Absence of real-time security log analytics and alerting components
tradeoffs: Edge tokenization isolates PCI scope but complicates dispute investigations in the portal

SEC-02.justification: Decisions, inputs, model identifiers, and explanations are streamed via DynamoDB Streams to S3 Object Lock with 7-year retention and KMS CMKs. Immutable records can be queried directly or via the portal well within one working day.
sensitivity_points: Query efficiency when retrieving historical records directly from long-term S3 storage
tradeoffs: Object Lock immutability guarantees regulatory compliance but restricts retroactive record modification or pruning
